message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
Here's tomorrow's route first, since it's the one with no slack.

## The route: B → A → C, and it's the only order that works

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** (20 min) |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B (done well before the 09:30 opening) ✅ |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A** (25 min) |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at A (within the 09:00–10:00 window) ✅ |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C** (40 min) |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break** (C won't accept until 11:00 anyway) |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at C ✅ |
| 12:00 | Back at depot (45 min) ✅ |

**Why the other orders fail**
- **A first:** he arrives at 09:00, finishes at 09:15, then reaches B at 09:40, after the shop opens.
- **C before A or B:** C can't take anything before 11:00, which pushes A and B too late.

**⚠️ He gets back at exactly 12:00, with zero slack.** The C drop can't start before 11:00, and C to depot is 45 minutes, so even a few minutes' delay at C makes him late. Before tomorrow:
- Ask C whether someone will be ready to receive at **11:00 sharp**.
- Check whether "back by 12:00" is a hard deadline or has some give.

## Van name ideas
- **Dovetail Dave**
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **The Chesterfield**
- **Veneer Vera**
- **Old Faithful**

## Friendlier "on the way" text
> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Business]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [15] minutes. See you soon!

## Three checks before handing over
1. **Condition:** inspect the surfaces, edges and finish for scratches, dents or marks from the journey, especially on freshly restored pieces.
2. **Completeness:** check that all parts are there, including handles, keys, shelves, glass, screws and fittings.
3. **Function and stability:** open drawers and doors, and check legs, joints and the piece's level once it's in position.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?
**Emailed, with the customer signing on the driver's phone,** and paper as a backup for customers who don't use email. That keeps a record you can't lose, and you'll have it immediately if there's ever a dispute.

## Proof of delivery, for the new part-timer
> **Proof of delivery** is the record, usually a signature, photo and time, showing that the customer received their item in good condition.

## Evening-before text (under 160 characters)
> Hi from [Business]! Your furniture is due tomorrow between 9:00 and 10:00. Any problems, just reply to this text. Thanks!

That's **111 characters** without the business name, so a name of up to about 49 characters keeps it to one message.

To keep it as a single text:
- **Avoid emojis, curly apostrophes and long dashes.** Any of these can switch the message to an encoding that limits a single text to 70 characters, which would split this one into two messages.
- **Watch the arrival window you fill in.** Changing "between 9:00 and 10:00" to longer wording also adds characters.
